description: A Single Mathematics B-style paper emphasizing cylindrical motion, oscillations, Fourier expansions, gradients, exact differentials, spherical integrals, and continuous distributions.
instructions: Show sufficient working to justify each answer.
Answers should be exact unless a numerical approximation is requested.
Begin each main question on a new page when working on paper.
label: Paper 1

questions.stem: A particle has cylindrical polar coordinates \(r=2+t\), \(\theta=t/2\), and \(z=t^2\), where \(t\ge0\). Its mass is \(m\).
questions.title: Cylindrical Motion and Work

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Write the Cartesian position of the particle and find its position at \(t=0\).
parts.answer: Use \(x=r\cos\theta\), \(y=r\sin\theta\), and \(z=z\). Since \(r=2+t\) and \(\theta=t/2\), \[\mathbf r(t)=((2+t)\cos(t/2),(2+t)\sin(t/2),t^2).\] At \(t=0\), this gives \[\mathbf r(0)=(2\cos0,2\sin0,0)=(2,0,0).\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the velocity in cylindrical components, and find the speed at \(t=2\).
parts.answer: In cylindrical coordinates, \[\mathbf v=\dot r\mathbf e_r+r\dot\theta\mathbf e_\theta+\dot z\mathbf e_z.\] Here \(\dot r=1\), \(\dot\theta=1/2\), and \(\dot z=2t\), so \[\mathbf v=\mathbf e_r+\frac{2+t}{2}\mathbf e_\theta+2t\mathbf e_z.\] The speed is \[|\mathbf v|=\sqrt{1^2+\left(\frac{2+t}{2}\right)^2+(2t)^2}.\] At \(t=2\), \[|\mathbf v(2)|=\sqrt{1+2^2+4^2}=\sqrt{21}.\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Find the acceleration in cylindrical components and hence the force at \(t=2\).
parts.answer: The cylindrical acceleration is \[\mathbf a=(\ddot r-r\dot\theta^2)\mathbf e_r+(r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta)\mathbf e_\theta+\ddot z\mathbf e_z.\] Here \(\ddot r=0\), \(\dot\theta=1/2\), \(\ddot\theta=0\), and \(\ddot z=2\). Therefore \[\mathbf a=-\frac{2+t}{4}\mathbf e_r+\mathbf e_\theta+2\mathbf e_z.\] At \(t=2\), \[\mathbf a(2)=-\mathbf e_r+\mathbf e_\theta+2\mathbf e_z,\] so \[\mathbf F(2)=m(-\mathbf e_r+\mathbf e_\theta+2\mathbf e_z).\]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Using the work-energy theorem, find the work done by the net force from \(t=0\) to \(t=2\).
parts.answer: The work-energy theorem gives \(W=\Delta K\). From part (b), \[|\mathbf v|^2=1+\frac{(2+t)^2}{4}+4t^2.\] At \(t=0\), \(|\mathbf v(0)|^2=1+1=2\). At \(t=2\), \(|\mathbf v(2)|^2=21\). Therefore \[W=\frac12m(21)-\frac12m(2)=\frac{19m}{2}.\]

questions.stem: Answer the following questions on homogeneous and forced second-order equations.
questions.title: Damped and Driven Oscillations

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The auxiliary equation is \[r^2+4r+5=0.\] Its roots are \(r=-2\pm i\). Hence \[y(t)=e^{-2t}(A\cos t+B\sin t).\] The condition \(y(0)=1\) gives \(A=1\). Differentiating, \[y'(t)=e^{-2t}\{(-A\sin t+B\cos t)-2(A\cos t+B\sin t)\}.\] At \(t=0\), this gives \(y'(0)=B-2A\). Since \(y'(0)=-1\) and \(A=1\), \(B-2=-1\), so \(B=1\). Therefore \[y(t)=e^{-2t}(\cos t+\sin t).\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Solve \(x''+x=3\cos2t\), subject to \(x(0)=0\) and \(x'(0)=0\).
parts.answer: The complementary solution is \(x_c=A\cos t+B\sin t\). Since the forcing frequency \(2\) is not the natural frequency \(1\), try \(x_p=C\cos2t\). Then \[x_p''+x_p=-4C\cos2t+C\cos2t=-3C\cos2t.\] Matching \(3\cos2t\) gives \(C=-1\), so \[x=A\cos t+B\sin t-\cos2t.\] The condition \(x(0)=0\) gives \(A-1=0\), so \(A=1\). Also \[x'=-A\sin t+B\cos t+2\sin2t,\] and \(x'(0)=B=0\). Therefore \[x(t)=\cos t-\cos2t.\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why the solution in part (b) does not contain a factor of \(t\).
parts.answer: A factor of \(t\) appears in the undamped method of undetermined coefficients when the forcing duplicates a complementary solution. Here the complementary frequency is \(1\), but the forcing term is \(3\cos2t\), with frequency \(2\). Since the forcing is not resonant with the natural mode, a bounded trial \(C\cos2t\) is sufficient and no factor of \(t\) is needed.

questions.stem: Let \(f(x)=x\) for \(0<x<2\), extended evenly to \((-2,2)\) and then periodically with period \(4\).
questions.title: Half-Range Cosine Expansion

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the extension and state the form of the Fourier series.
parts.answer: The even extension satisfies \(f(-x)=f(x)\), so it is \(|x|\) on \((-2,2)\). It is then repeated with period \(4\). Since the function is even, all sine coefficients are zero. With \(L=2\), the series has the form \[f(x)\sim\frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n\cos\frac{n\pi x}{2}.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the cosine coefficients and write the first three non-constant terms.
parts.answer: For a half-range cosine series on \((0,2)\), \[a_0=\frac{2}{2}\int_0^2x\,dx=2,\] so the constant term is \(a_0/2=1\). For \(n\ge1\), \[a_n=\frac{2}{2}\int_0^2x\cos\frac{n\pi x}{2}\,dx.\] Put \(k=n\pi/2\). Then \[\int_0^2x\cos kx\,dx=\left[\frac{x\sin kx}{k}+\frac{\cos kx}{k^2}\right]_0^2=\frac{(-1)^n-1}{k^2}.\] Hence \[a_n=\frac{4(((-1)^n)-1)}{n^2\pi^2}.\] Thus \(a_n=0\) for even \(n\), and \(a_n=-8/(n^2\pi^2)\) for odd \(n\). The first three non-constant terms are \[-\frac{8}{\pi^2}\cos\frac{\pi x}{2}-\frac{8}{9\pi^2}\cos\frac{3\pi x}{2}-\frac{8}{25\pi^2}\cos\frac{5\pi x}{2}.\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Use the value of the series at \(x=2\) to recover \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}1/(2k+1)^2\).
parts.answer: The even periodic extension is continuous at \(x=2\), so the Fourier series converges to \(f(2)=2\). Substituting \(x=2\) gives \[2=1+\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(-\frac{8}{(2k+1)^2\pi^2}\right)\cos((2k+1)\pi).\] For odd \(n\), \(\cos(n\pi)=-1\), so \[2=1+\frac{8}{\pi^2}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(2k+1)^2}.\] Therefore \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(2k+1)^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{8}.\]

questions.stem: The scalar field \(S(x,y)=30+x^2+xy-2y^2\) models a local calibration surface.
questions.title: Gradient Linearisation

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find \(\nabla S\) and the Hessian matrix, and evaluate both at \((1,1)\).
parts.answer: The first partial derivatives are \[S_x=2x+y,\qquad S_y=x-4y.\] Thus \[\nabla S=(2x+y,x-4y),\] and at \((1,1)\), \[\nabla S(1,1)=(3,-3).\] The second partial derivatives are \(S_{xx}=2\), \(S_{xy}=1\), and \(S_{yy}=-4\), so the Hessian is \[H=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&-4\end{pmatrix}.\] This Hessian is constant, so it has the same value at \((1,1)\).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the first-order linear approximation near \((1,1)\), and use it to estimate \(S(1.1,0.9)\).
parts.answer: First compute \[S(1,1)=30+1+1-2=30.\] The first-order linear approximation is \[L(x,y)=30+3(x-1)-3(y-1).\] At \((1.1,0.9)\), this gives \[L(1.1,0.9)=30+3(0.1)-3(-0.1)=30.6.\] Therefore the first-order estimate is \(30.6\).

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Use the second-order Taylor correction to improve the estimate in part (b).
parts.answer: The displacement from \((1,1)\) to \((1.1,0.9)\) is \(\mathbf h=(0.1,-0.1)\). The second-order correction is \[\frac12\mathbf h^TH\mathbf h.\] Since \[H\mathbf h=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&-4\end{pmatrix}\binom{0.1}{-0.1}=\binom{0.1}{0.5},\] we have \[\mathbf h^TH\mathbf h=(0.1,-0.1)\cdot(0.1,0.5)=0.01-0.05=-0.04.\] The correction is \(-0.02\). Therefore the improved estimate is \[30.6-0.02=30.58.\]

questions.section: Section E: Critical Points and Vector Calculus
questions.stem: Consider the differential \(d\Phi=(3x^2+2ay)\,dx+(bx+4y)\,dy\) and the vector fields \(\mathbf F=(xz,-yz,x^2+y^2)\) and \(\mathbf A=(xy,yz,zx)\).
questions.title: Exact Differential and Solenoidal Field

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the condition on \(a\) and \(b\) for \(d\Phi\) to be exact, and find \(\Phi\) when this condition holds.
parts.answer: Write \(M=3x^2+2ay\) and \(N=bx+4y\). Exactness requires \(M_y=N_x\). Here \[M_y=2a,\qquad N_x=b.\] Therefore the condition is \(b=2a\). When this holds, integrate \(M\) with respect to \(x\): \[\Phi=x^3+2axy+g(y).\] Differentiating with respect to \(y\), \[\Phi_y=2ax+g'(y).\] Since \(N=2ax+4y\), we need \(g'(y)=4y\), so \(g(y)=2y^2+C\). Thus \[\Phi=x^3+2axy+2y^2+C.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Show that \(\mathbf F\) is solenoidal by computing its divergence.
parts.answer: A vector field is solenoidal when its divergence is zero. For \(\mathbf F=(xz,-yz,x^2+y^2)\), \[\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(xz)+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(-yz)+\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(x^2+y^2).\] This gives \[\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=z-z+0=0.\] Therefore \(\mathbf F\) is solenoidal.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt:
Compute \(
abla	imes\mathbf A\), and verify directly that \(
abla\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf A)=0\).
parts.answer:
With \(\mathbf A=(P,Q,R)=(xy,yz,zx)\), \[
abla	imes\mathbf A=(R_y-Q_z,\ P_z-R_x,\ Q_x-P_y).\] Since \(R_y=0\), \(Q_z=y\), \(P_z=0\), \(R_x=z\), \(Q_x=0\), and \(P_y=x\), \[
abla	imes\mathbf A=(-y,-z,-x).\] Now take the divergence: \[
abla\cdot(-y,-z,-x)= rac{\partial(-y)}{\partial x}+ rac{\partial(-z)}{\partial y}+ rac{\partial(-x)}{\partial z}=0+0+0=0.\] This directly verifies the identity for this field.

questions.section: Section F: Multiple Integrals and Vector Identities
questions.stem: Let \(E\) be the solid inside the sphere \(\rho\le3\) and inside the cone \(0\le\phi\le\pi/4\), using spherical coordinates with volume element \(dV=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta\).
questions.title: Cone Integral in Spherical Coordinates

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Write bounds for \(E\) in spherical coordinates and state the volume element.
parts.answer: The solid is rotationally symmetric about the \(z\)-axis, so \(\theta\) runs through a full turn. The sphere gives \(0\le\rho\le3\), and the cone gives \(0\le\phi\le\pi/4\). Thus \[0\le\theta\le2\pi,\qquad 0\le\phi\le\frac{\pi}{4},\qquad 0\le\rho\le3.\] The spherical volume element is \[dV=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Evaluate the volume of \(E\).
parts.answer: The volume is \[V=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/4}\int_0^3\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta.\] Evaluate each factor: \[\int_0^3\rho^2\,d\rho=9,\qquad \int_0^{\pi/4}\sin\phi\,d\phi=1-\frac{\sqrt2}{2},\qquad \int_0^{2\pi}d\theta=2\pi.\] Hence \[V=18\pi\left(1-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)=9\pi(2-\sqrt2).\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Evaluate \(\iiint_E \rho^2\,dV\) and explain why the factor \(\rho^2\sin\phi\) is needed.
parts.answer: Using the same bounds, \[\iiint_E\rho^2\,dV=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/4}\int_0^3\rho^2(\rho^2\sin\phi)\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta.\] Thus \[\iiint_E\rho^2\,dV=2\pi\left(1-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)\left[\frac{\rho^5}{5}\right]_0^3=\frac{486\pi}{5}\left(1-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right).\] Equivalently this is \[\frac{243\pi}{5}(2-\sqrt2).\] The factor \(\rho^2\sin\phi\) is the spherical Jacobian: it converts coordinate increments into physical volume.

questions.stem: A sensor output \(X\) is modelled by the density \(f_X(x)=c x(2-x)\) for \(0\le x\le2\), and \(0\) otherwise.
questions.title: Measurement Distribution

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the constant \(c\).
parts.answer: A density must integrate to \(1\). Therefore \[1=\int_0^2c x(2-x)\,dx=c\int_0^2(2x-x^2)\,dx.\] The integral is \[\left[x^2-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2=4-\frac83=\frac43.\] Hence \(c\cdot4/3=1\), so \[c=\frac34.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find \(E[X]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).
parts.answer: Using \(c=3/4\), \[E[X]=\int_0^2x\cdot\frac34x(2-x)\,dx=\frac34\int_0^2(2x^2-x^3)\,dx.\] This gives \[E[X]=\frac34\left(\frac{16}{3}-4\right)=1.\] Also \[E[X^2]=\frac34\int_0^2(2x^3-x^4)\,dx=\frac34\left(8-\frac{32}{5}\right)=\frac65.\] Therefore \[\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2=\frac65-1=\frac15.\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: For \(45\) independent sensor readings, use a normal approximation to estimate \(P(\bar X>1.1)\).
parts.answer: The sample mean has mean \(1\) and variance \[(1/5)/45=\frac{1}{225}.\] Therefore its standard deviation is \(1/15\). By a normal approximation, \[P(\bar X>1.1)\approx P\left(Z>\frac{1.1-1}{1/15}\right)=P(Z>1.5).\] From standard normal tables this is approximately \(0.0668\).

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Find \(P(X>1.5)\), and explain why \(P(X=1.5)=0\).
parts.answer: For a continuous random variable, an exact single value has zero probability, so \(P(X=1.5)=0\). The tail probability is an area: \[P(X>1.5)=\int_{1.5}^{2}\frac34x(2-x)\,dx.\] Since \[\int x(2-x)\,dx=x^2-\frac{x^3}{3},\] we get \[P(X>1.5)=\frac34\left(\frac43-\frac98\right)=\frac34\cdot\frac{5}{24}=\frac{5}{32}.\]
